# Check reference

**81 checks**: 27 bugs · 15 efficiency · 10 structure · 14 standards · 15 security. By severity: 29 high · 36 medium · 16 low.

`mast explain <check-id>` prints the same reasoning in the terminal. Every check can be switched off per project (`analysis.ignore`) or per line (`# mast: ignore[<check-id>]`) — see [the analyzer](analyzer.md#turning-a-check-off).

Severity decides what blocks: **high** findings stop a write and gate the end of a turn by default, **medium** and **low** are reported for Claude to fix as it works.

## Bugs

Defects that make the code do the wrong thing at runtime. This is the bug hunter.

### `bug/assert-for-validation`

**`assert` used outside tests** · high

Assertions are removed when Python runs with -O, which is common in production images. Validation written as an assert therefore disappears exactly where it matters, and untrusted input flows straight through.

**Fix.** Raise explicitly: `if not ok: raise ValueError(...)`. Keep `assert` for tests and for invariants you are happy to lose.

### `bug/bare-except`

**Bare `except:`** · high

A bare except also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, so Ctrl-C and process shutdown are swallowed, and genuine programming errors are hidden instead of surfacing.

**Fix.** Catch what you can handle: `except (ValueError, KeyError):`, or `except Exception:` when you truly mean any application error.

### `bug/blocking-call-in-async`

**Blocking call inside `async def`** · high

A synchronous call inside a coroutine blocks the event loop, freezing every other request in the process. Under load this looks like a mysterious latency cliff rather than an error.

**Fix.** Use the async equivalent, or push the blocking work to a thread with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`.

### `bug/comparison-to-none`

**`== None` instead of `is None`** · low

Equality calls `__eq__`, which a custom class (or a numpy array / ORM field) can redefine, so the test may not mean what it says.

**Fix.** Use `is None` / `is not None`.

### `bug/constant-in-condition`

**Literal used as a condition** · high

`if x == 1 or 2:` reads like 'x is 1 or 2' but means 'x == 1, or the truthy value 2' — always true. The branch fires for every input and the intended comparison never happens.

**Fix.** Compare explicitly (`x == 1 or x == 2`) or test membership (`x in (1, 2)`).

### `bug/duplicate-condition`

**Duplicated branch condition** · high

The second identical condition in an if/elif chain can never be reached, so the code it guards is dead and the case it was meant to handle falls through.

**Fix.** Correct the duplicated test, or merge the branches if they really are the same case.

### `bug/duplicate-key`

**Duplicate key in a literal** · medium

A repeated key in a dict or set literal silently discards the earlier entry, so configuration or mapping data quietly loses a value.

**Fix.** Remove or rename the duplicate.

### `bug/handler-order`

**Unreachable exception handler** · high

Handlers are tried in order, so a broad handler listed first catches everything a narrower one below it was written for. The specific recovery code never runs — and nobody notices until the specific failure happens in production.

**Fix.** Order handlers narrowest first, with `except Exception:` last.

### `bug/identity-comparison`

**`is` compared against a literal** · high

`is` compares object identity, not value. It appears to work for small ints and short strings because CPython interns them, then fails for the same value computed a different way — a bug that only shows up with real data.

**Fix.** Use `==` for values; keep `is` for `None`, `True`, `False` and sentinels.

### `bug/implicit-string-concat`

**Implicit string concatenation — probably a missing comma** · medium

Two adjacent string literals are joined into one, so a missing comma in a list silently merges two entries. The collection ends up one element short with a corrupted value, and nothing raises.

**Fix.** Add the missing comma. When the join is deliberate, end the first part with a space so the intent is visible, or use explicit `+`.

### `bug/late-binding-closure`

**Closure captures the loop variable** · high

A function defined in a loop captures the loop variable by reference, not by value. Every closure created in the loop sees the final value, so callbacks, partials and deferred tasks all act on the last item instead of the one they were created for.

**Fix.** Bind the value at definition time — `lambda x=item: f(x)` — or use `functools.partial(f, item)`.

### `bug/lru-cache-on-method`

**`lru_cache` on an instance method** · medium

The cache is stored on the function, so `self` becomes part of the key and every instance that was ever cached is kept alive forever — a steady memory leak, plus stale results when the instance changes.

**Fix.** Cache a module-level function of plain values, use `functools.cached_property`, or clear the cache per instance.

### `bug/missing-f-prefix`

**Placeholder in a plain string** · medium

A string containing `{name}` without the `f` prefix is never interpolated. Logs, messages and queries ship the literal braces instead of the value, so the useful detail is lost.

**Fix.** Add the `f` prefix, or call `.format(...)` if the template is filled in later.

### `bug/missing-super-init`

**Subclass `__init__` never calls `super().__init__()`** · medium

Skipping the parent initialiser leaves the base class's attributes unset. The object looks valid until a base-class method runs and fails on missing state, often far from this file.

**Fix.** Call `super().__init__(...)` — usually first — in the subclass `__init__`.

### `bug/mutable-default`

**Mutable default argument** · high

Default arguments are evaluated once, when the function is defined. A list, dict or set default is therefore shared by every call, so state leaks between unrelated callers — a classic source of 'impossible' production bugs that tests with a single call never reproduce.

**Fix.** Default to `None` and build the container inside the body: `def f(items=None): items = [] if items is None else items`.

### `bug/mutate-during-iteration`

**Collection mutated while iterating it** · high

Adding to or removing from a list, dict or set while looping over it skips elements or raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`. The skipped items are silent — the loop simply misses records.

**Fix.** Iterate over a copy (`for x in list(items):`) or build the result in a new collection and replace it afterwards.

### `bug/naive-utcnow`

**Naive UTC timestamp** · medium

`datetime.utcnow()` returns a naive datetime that claims no timezone while holding UTC. Compared with an aware timestamp it raises, and stored in a local-time column it silently shifts by hours. It is deprecated from Python 3.12.

**Fix.** Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` (or `datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, timezone.utc)`) and keep datetimes aware end to end.

### `bug/return-in-finally`

**`return` or `break` in a `finally` block** · high

A `finally` block that returns or breaks discards any exception in flight. Failures vanish without a traceback and callers see a normal return value for work that never completed.

**Fix.** Put the value in a variable and return it after the `try`, leaving `finally` for cleanup only.

### `bug/self-assignment`

**Variable assigned to itself** · medium

A self-assignment does nothing. It usually means an attribute, parameter or index on one side was mistyped, so the real value is never stored.

**Fix.** Assign the value you meant, e.g. `self.total = total`.

### `bug/self-comparison`

**Expression compared with itself** · medium

Comparing a value with itself is always the same answer, so the guard it protects is either dead or the wrong variable was typed.

**Fix.** Compare against the value you meant — usually a neighbouring variable or attribute.

### `bug/shared-class-attribute`

**Mutable class attribute shared by all instances** · medium

A list or dict defined in the class body belongs to the class, not the instance. Every object appends to the same container, so data from one request, user or tenant shows up in another.

**Fix.** Assign it in `__init__`, or use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=list)`.

### `bug/silent-except`

**Exception silently swallowed** · medium

An except block that only passes discards the error and its traceback. The failure still happened, but nothing records it — the bug resurfaces later as corrupt data or an empty screen with no trail.

**Fix.** Log it (`logger.exception(...)`), re-raise, or return an explicit fallback. If ignoring is correct, say why in a comment.

### `bug/syntax-error`

**File does not parse** · high

A module with a syntax error cannot be imported, tested or deployed — every other check is blind on it.

**Fix.** Fix the syntax error the message points at. The analyzer reports the position Python itself rejects.

### `bug/type-equality`

**Types compared with `==`** · low

`type(x) == T` rejects subclasses, so legitimate values fail the check — a frequent cause of 'works with my class, not with theirs'.

**Fix.** Use `isinstance(x, T)` (or `is` when you deliberately want the exact class).

### `bug/unclosed-resource`

**File opened without a context manager** · medium

Without `with`, the file handle is released only when the garbage collector gets to it. On an exception the write is never flushed, and long-running processes run out of descriptors.

**Fix.** Use `with open(...) as f:` — or `contextlib.closing` for objects without context-manager support.

### `bug/unraised-exception`

**Exception created but not raised** · high

Constructing an exception has no effect on its own. The error path silently continues as if everything succeeded, and the caller gets a success result for a failed operation.

**Fix.** Add `raise`: `raise ValueError(...)`.

### `bug/unreachable-code`

**Unreachable statement** · medium

Code after a `return`, `raise`, `continue` or `break` in the same block never executes. It is usually a real mistake — cleanup, a log line or the actual result left stranded behind an early exit.

**Fix.** Move the statement above the exit, or delete it if it is dead.


## Efficiency

Correct code that does avoidable work — usually an accidental O(n²) or a query per row.

### `perf/append-only-loop`

**Loop that only appends** · low

A loop whose entire body is one `append` is a comprehension written the long way: more lines, a per-iteration method lookup, and less obvious intent.

**Fix.** Use a comprehension: `result = [transform(x) for x in items if keep(x)]`.

### `perf/await-in-loop`

**Sequential `await` in a loop** · low

Awaiting one call per iteration serialises work that could overlap, so total latency is the sum of every round trip instead of the slowest one.

**Fix.** Collect the coroutines and `await asyncio.gather(*tasks)` — keep the loop only when each step depends on the previous result.

### `perf/count-for-membership`

**`.count()` used as a membership test** · low

`count()` always scans the whole sequence; `in` stops at the first match.

**Fix.** Use `if value in items:`.

### `perf/deepcopy-in-loop`

**`deepcopy` inside a loop** · low

A deep copy walks the entire object graph. Per iteration it dominates the loop, and it is usually defensive rather than needed.

**Fix.** Copy once outside the loop, copy only the part you mutate, or build new immutable values instead.

### `perf/dict-keys-membership`

**`in d.keys()` instead of `in d`** · low

`in d` hashes the key directly; going through `.keys()` builds a view first and reads as though the dict were a list.

**Fix.** Drop `.keys()`: `if key in mapping:`.

### `perf/identity-comprehension`

**Comprehension that copies without transforming** · low

`[x for x in items]` walks the sequence in Python just to produce the same values a constructor would copy in C.

**Fix.** Use `list(items)` / `set(items)` / `dict(mapping)`.

### `perf/list-membership-literal`

**Membership test against a list or tuple literal** · low

A literal sequence is scanned element by element; a set literal hashes once. With several options the set is both faster and clearer about intent.

**Fix.** Use a set literal: `if value in {"a", "b", "c"}:`.

### `perf/loop-string-concat`

**String built by repeated concatenation in a loop** · high

Strings are immutable, so `s += part` copies the whole accumulated string on every iteration. The loop is quadratic: fine for ten rows, minutes of CPU for a large export.

**Fix.** Append the pieces to a list and `''.join(parts)` once, or write straight to a buffer/stream.

### `perf/n-plus-one-query`

**Database query inside a loop** · high

One query per iteration is the N+1 problem: a page that looks instant with 10 rows issues hundreds of round trips in production. It is the single most common cause of slow enterprise endpoints.

**Fix.** Fetch the rows in one query before the loop (`filter(id__in=ids)`, a join, `select_related`/`selectinload`) and index the result in memory.

### `perf/pandas-concat-in-loop`

**DataFrame grown inside a loop** · high

`concat`/`append` in a loop reallocates and copies the whole frame on every iteration, making the build quadratic. (`DataFrame.append` was also removed in pandas 2.)

**Fix.** Collect the pieces in a list and call `pd.concat(frames)` once after the loop.

### `perf/pandas-row-loop`

**Row-by-row loop over a DataFrame** · high

`iterrows`/`itertuples`/`apply(axis=1)` run Python per row and rebuild a Series each time — often 100× slower than the vectorised equivalent, and the gap grows with the data.

**Fix.** Use vectorised column operations, `np.where`, `groupby`/`merge`, or `.to_numpy()` for the numeric core.

### `perf/quadratic-membership`

**Membership test against a list inside a loop** · high

`x in some_list` scans the list. Inside a loop that is O(n·m): a pair of 10k-row collections turns into 100 million comparisons, which is the difference between 20ms and half a minute.

**Fix.** Build a `set` (or dict) once before the loop and test membership against it.

### `perf/range-len`

**`range(len(x))` index loop** · low

Indexing through `range(len(...))` re-reads the sequence on every access and hides what is being iterated.

**Fix.** Iterate the items (`for item in items:`) or use `enumerate(items)` when the index is needed.

### `perf/redundant-call`

**Redundant intermediate collection** · low

Materialising a list only to hand it to another call allocates the whole sequence for nothing, and hides what the code actually wants.

**Fix.** Drop the wrapper: `sorted(x)`, `len(x)`, `min(x)`, `next(iter(x))`, `sum(x for x in ...)`.

### `perf/regex-compile-in-loop`

**Regex compiled inside a loop** · medium

`re.compile` parses the pattern each time. In a loop or a hot function that cost is paid per row, for a value that never changes.

**Fix.** Compile once at module level (`PATTERN = re.compile(...)`) and reuse it.


## Structure

Size, complexity, duplication and coupling: what makes the code expensive to change.

### `structure/deep-nesting`

**Deeply nested blocks** · medium

Every level of nesting is a condition the reader must keep on the stack. Deep nesting is where off-by-one and wrong-branch bugs hide.

**Fix.** Invert conditions and return early, extract the inner block into a function, or use `continue` to skip cases in loops.

### `structure/duplicate-block`

**Duplicated function body** · medium

Two functions with the same shape mean a fix has to be found twice. In practice one copy gets updated and the other keeps the bug, which is how behaviour silently diverges between call sites.

**Fix.** Extract the shared body into one function and parameterise what differs.

### `structure/high-complexity`

**Function has too many branches** · medium

Cyclomatic complexity counts the independent paths through a function. Past ~10, the paths cannot all be covered by tests or held in mind, and each new condition multiplies the untested combinations.

**Fix.** Return early to flatten guards, move branch bodies into functions, or replace the branching with a lookup table or polymorphism.

### `structure/import-cycle`

**Circular import between modules** · high

Modules that import each other can only be loaded in one order. The result is an `ImportError` or a half-initialised module that depends on which entry point ran first — and it breaks in production long before it breaks in a test.

**Fix.** Extract the shared types into a third module, import inside the function that needs it, or invert the dependency with a protocol.

### `structure/large-class`

**Class has too many methods** · medium

A class with dozens of methods is several classes sharing a namespace: unrelated features change the same file, tests need the whole object built, and nothing can be reused separately.

**Fix.** Split by responsibility — the methods that touch the same attributes belong together.

### `structure/large-module`

**Module is too long** · low

A very long module is a merge-conflict magnet and hides its own structure: nobody can see what belongs with what.

**Fix.** Split it into a package of focused modules along the seams the imports already suggest.

### `structure/long-function`

**Function is too long** · medium

A function longer than a screen cannot be held in your head at once, so reviewers skim it and changes are made by local patching. Length is also the strongest predictor of defect density.

**Fix.** Extract the cohesive steps into named helpers — usually the blocks you would otherwise write a comment above.

### `structure/too-many-arguments`

**Function takes too many arguments** · medium

A long parameter list means the function has many reasons to change and callers must get an exact order right. Positional mistakes between same-typed arguments are silent.

**Fix.** Group related parameters into a dataclass or TypedDict, or split the function. Make the rest keyword-only with `*`.

### `structure/too-many-locals`

**Function juggles too many local variables** · low

A large number of locals usually means several concerns share one scope, so a reader cannot tell which variables belong to which step.

**Fix.** Extract each concern into its own function so its variables live and die there.

### `structure/wildcard-import`

**Wildcard import** · medium

`from x import *` makes it impossible to tell where a name came from, lets an upstream release shadow local names silently, and defeats every static analysis tool including your IDE.

**Fix.** Import the names you use explicitly.


## Enterprise standards

Typed public APIs, real exceptions, real logging, no hidden shared state.

### `api/any-annotation`

**`Any` in a public signature** · low

`Any` switches type checking off at that boundary, so errors pass straight through the layer that was supposed to validate them.

**Fix.** Use a concrete type, a `Protocol` for duck typing, a `TypeVar` for generics, or `object` when you truly accept anything.

### `api/global-mutable-state`

**Module-level mutable state** · medium

A module-level list or dict that the code mutates is process-wide shared state: it leaks between requests, breaks under threads and workers, and makes tests order-dependent — the classic 'passes alone, fails in the suite'.

**Fix.** Pass the state explicitly, hold it on an instance, or use a proper cache/store with a defined lifetime.

### `api/missing-docstring`

**Public API has no docstring** · low

The docstring is where the contract that types cannot express lives: units, error behaviour, side effects. Without it callers read the body and depend on incidental detail.

**Fix.** Add a short docstring saying what it does, what it raises, and anything surprising. Skip the obvious getters.

### `api/missing-type-hints`

**Public function is not fully annotated** · medium

Type hints are the contract a caller reads and the only thing a type checker can verify. Without them refactors are guesswork across module boundaries, and a whole class of integration bug reaches runtime that mypy would have caught in CI.

**Fix.** Annotate every parameter and the return type. Use `-> None` for procedures and `Protocol`/`TypedDict` for structural inputs.

### `api/mutable-dataclass-default`

**Mutable default on a dataclass field** · medium

A mutable default on a class-level field is shared by every instance that does not override it, so one object's mutation shows up in the next. `dataclass` rejects the obvious cases at import time and silently accepts the rest (custom objects, pydantic v1 models).

**Fix.** Use `field(default_factory=list)` / `default_factory=dict` (or `Field(default_factory=...)` in pydantic).

### `api/sys-exit-in-library`

**`sys.exit()` in library code** · medium

Killing the process from inside a library takes the decision away from the caller: a web worker, test runner or notebook is terminated instead of handling the error.

**Fix.** Raise an exception and let the entry point (CLI `main`, request handler) decide the exit code.

### `api/unfinished-code`

**Unfinished implementation left behind** · medium

A stub that raises `NotImplementedError` or silently passes looks complete to the caller and to review, then fails in production on the first real input.

**Fix.** Finish it, or keep it abstract (`@abstractmethod` on an ABC/Protocol) so the type checker refuses incomplete subclasses.

### `err/bare-exception-class`

**Generic `Exception` raised** · medium

`raise Exception('failed')` forces every caller to catch everything or parse the message. Callers cannot distinguish a validation problem from an outage, so retry and error-reporting logic cannot be written.

**Fix.** Raise a specific builtin (`ValueError`, `PermissionError`, `TimeoutError`) or a domain exception from your own base class.

### `err/broad-except`

**`except Exception` without handling it** · medium

Catching everything and carrying on hides programming errors — a typo'd attribute is treated like a network timeout. The system keeps running in an undefined state instead of failing where the fault is.

**Fix.** Catch the specific exceptions you can recover from. If you must catch broadly, log with `logger.exception(...)` and re-raise or return an explicit error.

### `err/lost-traceback`

**Exception re-raised without `from`** · medium

Raising a new exception inside an `except` block without `from` hides the original cause. The traceback shows your wrapper and not the line that actually failed, which is exactly the line you need at 3am.

**Fix.** Use `raise MyError(...) from exc` — or `from None` when hiding the cause is deliberate.

### `log/eager-formatting`

**Log message formatted before the level check** · low

An f-string is built whether or not the level is enabled, so debug logging costs CPU in production. It also loses the structured arguments that log aggregators group duplicate messages by.

**Fix.** Pass the values as arguments: `logger.info("user %s saved", user_id)`.

### `log/error-without-traceback`

**Error logged without its traceback** · medium

`logger.error(str(exc))` records one line and throws the stack away, so the log says what broke but not where. Debugging then needs a reproduction instead of the log you already have.

**Fix.** Inside an `except` block use `logger.exception("...")` (or `logger.error(..., exc_info=True)`).

### `log/print-in-code`

**`print()` used for output in application code** · medium

`print` has no level, no timestamp, no request context and no destination control, so it is invisible to log aggregation and cannot be turned down. In a service it is output nobody will ever see.

**Fix.** Use a module logger: `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` and `logger.info(...)`. Keep `print` for CLI output.

### `log/root-logger`

**Root logger used directly** · medium

`logging.info(...)` writes to the root logger, so the message carries no module name and cannot be filtered or levelled per component. It also configures logging as a side effect of the first call.

**Fix.** Create a module logger once: `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)`.


## Security

The Python-specific footguns that turn into incidents.

### `sec/debug-enabled`

**Debug mode enabled in source** · high

Debug mode serves tracebacks with source, local variables and settings to anyone who triggers an error, and in Flask/Werkzeug it can expose an interactive console. Committed as `True`, it ships.

**Fix.** Read it from the environment and default to off: `DEBUG = os.environ.get("DEBUG") == "1"`.

### `sec/eval-exec`

**`eval` / `exec` on a non-literal** · high

Evaluating a string executes arbitrary Python with full process privileges. Any path from user input, a database row or a config file to this call is remote code execution.

**Fix.** Parse the data instead: `json.loads`, `ast.literal_eval`, or an explicit dispatch dict mapping names to functions.

### `sec/hardcoded-secret`

**Credential hardcoded in source** · high

A secret in source is a secret in git history, in every clone and in every CI log. Rotating it means rewriting history, and the leak usually outlives the person who added it.

**Fix.** Read it from the environment or a secret manager: `os.environ["DB_PASSWORD"]`. Keep a placeholder in `.env.example` instead.

### `sec/insecure-temp-file`

**Predictable temporary file** · medium

`mktemp` only returns a name, so another process can create or swap that path before you open it (a TOCTOU race) and have your code write to, or read, a file it controls.

**Fix.** Use `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile()` or `tempfile.mkstemp()`, which create the file atomically.

### `sec/jwt-unverified`

**Token signature not verified** · high

Decoding a JWT without verifying the signature means anyone can mint a token with any claims — it is authentication that authenticates nothing.

**Fix.** Verify with the expected key and algorithms: `jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["RS256"], audience=...)`.

### `sec/os-system`

**`os.system` / `os.popen` used** · high

These always run a shell, give no way to pass arguments safely, and discard the exit status detail — every input becomes shell syntax.

**Fix.** Use `subprocess.run([...], check=True, capture_output=True)` with an argument list.

### `sec/permissive-cors`

**CORS allows any origin** · medium

`*` lets any site call the API from a visitor's browser. Combined with cookie credentials it is a cross-site request forgery hole that bypasses same-origin protection entirely.

**Fix.** List the origins you serve, and never pair a wildcard with `allow_credentials=True`.

### `sec/random-for-secrets`

**`random` used to generate a secret** · medium

`random` is a predictable Mersenne Twister seeded from the clock. An attacker who sees a few outputs can reconstruct the state and derive every token you issue.

**Fix.** Use `secrets.token_urlsafe()`, `secrets.token_hex()` or `secrets.choice()`.

### `sec/shell-injection`

**Shell command built from a dynamic string** · high

With `shell=True` the string is parsed by the shell, so `;`, `|`, backticks and `$(...)` in any interpolated value execute as commands with the process's privileges.

**Fix.** Pass an argument list and drop `shell=True`: `subprocess.run(["git", "clone", url], check=True)`. If the shell is unavoidable, quote with `shlex.quote`.

### `sec/sql-injection`

**SQL built by string interpolation** · high

Any value spliced into SQL text can end the string literal and append its own statement. This is the oldest remote-takeover bug there is, and an f-string makes it look tidy.

**Fix.** Pass parameters to the driver: `cursor.execute("... WHERE id = %s", (user_id,))`, or use the ORM's query API. Never format the value in.

### `sec/tls-verification-disabled`

**TLS certificate verification disabled** · high

With verification off, any machine on the path can present its own certificate and read or rewrite the traffic. It usually starts as a workaround for a staging certificate and ships to production.

**Fix.** Keep `verify=True` and install the correct CA bundle (`verify="/path/to/ca.pem"` for an internal CA).

### `sec/unsafe-deserialization`

**Untrusted data deserialized into objects** · high

`pickle`, `yaml.load` and `marshal` reconstruct arbitrary objects, which means they can be made to call arbitrary code while loading. Caches, queues and uploaded files are all attacker-reachable.

**Fix.** Use `json` for data, `yaml.safe_load` for YAML, and a schema (pydantic, dataclass + validation) to rebuild objects.

### `sec/unsafe-markup`

**HTML escaping bypassed** · high

Marking a computed string as safe turns any value inside it into HTML, so user content becomes script — stored XSS that runs with the victim's session.

**Fix.** Let the template escape it. If markup must be composed, build it with `format_html(...)` or sanitise with a allowlist (`bleach`, `nh3`).

### `sec/unsafe-xml`

**XML parsed with the standard library** · medium

The stdlib XML parsers resolve external entities and expand nested ones, so untrusted XML can read local files (XXE) or exhaust memory (billion laughs) before your code sees any data.

**Fix.** Parse untrusted XML with `defusedxml` (`from defusedxml.ElementTree import parse`).

### `sec/weak-hash`

**Broken hash used for security** · medium

MD5 and SHA-1 are collision-broken: two different inputs can be made to hash the same, so they cannot back a signature, token or integrity check.

**Fix.** Use SHA-256+ for integrity, and `bcrypt`/`argon2`/`scrypt` for passwords. For non-security uses pass `usedforsecurity=False`.
